claims.text: At lower temperatures, nanoscale precipitates or solute friction maintain dislocation-based yielding.
Increasing temperature produces a transition from dislocation glide to diffusion-controlled deformation.
Activation of diffusion-controlled mechanisms at high temperature makes yield strength insensitive to strain rate.
The investigated material is a quaternary equiatomic, single-phase FCC random solid solution.
Processing history may introduce nanoscale oxides or coherent precipitates into the alloy.
Tensile deformation can produce dislocation cell structures and wavy or zigzag dislocations.
Deformation may produce nanotwins or an FCC-to-HCP phase transformation.
Lattice-parameter differences among constituent atoms generate friction that hinders partial-dislocation motion.
Low-temperature plasticity is governed by dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Low-temperature yield strength is strain-rate sensitive.
At high temperature, deformation proceeds through diffusion-controlled dislocation creep and grain-boundary sliding.
Cryogenic deformation significantly increases both yield strength and ductility.
Above 800 K, yield strength plateaus or has negligible dependence on strain rate.
As temperature rises from about 800 K to 1000 K, dislocation configurations evolve from cell structures to wavy or zigzag structures.
Standard equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloys typically have high strain-rate sensitivity at room temperature.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi transitions from dislocation glide near 800 K to diffusion-controlled dislocation creep near 1000 K.
Moderate-to-high stacking-fault energy permits dislocation cross-slip in the proposed boundary regime.
A dominant deformation-induced BCC or HCP martensitic transformation may invalidate the proposed dislocation-to-diffusion transition.
A strain-rate sensitivity exponent greater than 0.05 at 900 K would falsify the proposed high-temperature strain-rate-insensitive regime.
Observation only of glide structures, without climb or other diffusion-assisted configurations at 900 K, would falsify the diffusion-controlled mechanism.

contradictions.description: The target is repeatedly described as quaternary, but CoCrFeMnNi is a five-element alloy, and AlxCoCrFeNi is also five-element when x is nonzero. No definite quaternary elemental composition is supplied.

The material is called a single-phase random solid solution while also being allowed to contain coherent precipitates or nanoscale oxide phases; those constituents would make the overall microstructure multiphase unless 'single phase' is restricted explicitly to the matrix.
